cards.front: What is a neuroblast in the fly embryo?
cards.back: A neural stem cell that moves inward from an ectodermal proneural cluster.
cards.quote: From each cluster one cell moves inward as a neuroblast, a neural stem cell of the fly embryo.

cards.front: In a fly proneural cluster, how do neural competence and precursor selection differ?
cards.back: Proneural factors make cells able to become neural; Notch signaling compares neighbours to select precursors. Between two initially alike cells, this breaks the tie only if the feedback loop is steep.
cards.quote: In the fly, proneural factors say which cells may become neural; Notch says which one does, by comparing each cell with its neighbours.

cards.front: Proneural genes encode {{c1::basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH)}} transcription factors.
cards.quote: All of these genes encode basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factors.

cards.front: Which parts of a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor mediate protein pairing and DNA binding?
cards.back: The helix-loop-helix region mediates pairing; the basic region binds DNA at an E-box.
cards.quote: The helix-loop-helix part lets two proteins pair; the basic part grips DNA at a short sequence called an E-box.

cards.front: In staged fly embryos, an achaete-expressing cluster is competent; the later selected cell with high achaete is {{c1::determined}}.
cards.quote: It came on in clusters of a few cells; later one cell in each cluster held much more achaete RNA and became the neural progenitor.

cards.front: A fly expresses achaete and scute in additional locations. What happens to bristle formation, and why?
cards.back: Extra bristles form because these proneural genes can confer the competence needed to produce bristles at additional sites.
cards.quote: are needed for bristles: remove them and bristles are missing; switch them on in extra places and extra bristles form.

cards.front: After Notch is deleted in fly embryos, achaete clusters retain their positions but fail to restrict high expression to one cell. Which developmental step requires Notch?
cards.back: Selection within a cluster requires Notch. Initial cluster placement persists without it, separating placement from the restriction of precursor fate.
cards.quote: The clusters still formed in their normal places, but high achaete expression was no longer restricted to one cell in each cluster.

cards.front: The membrane ligand Delta activates {{c1::Notch}} on a touching cell.
cards.quote: Delta, a membrane protein on one cell, binds Notch on the cell it touches and pulls.

cards.front: In fly proneural clusters, Notch induces the {{c1::Enhancer of split (E(spl))}} genes, which encode proneural repressors.
cards.quote: In a proneural cluster the targets that matter are the Enhancer of split, or E(spl), genes.

cards.front: How does Delta on one fly cell reduce proneural expression in its neighbour?
cards.back: Delta activates the neighbour’s Notch. Cleavage releases the Notch inner domain, which enters the nucleus and works with CSL to induce E(spl) repressors.
cards.quote: They encode bHLH repressors that switch proneural genes off.

cards.front: Why can mutual inhibition between two cells reinforce an initial difference?
cards.back: The stronger sender suppresses its neighbour, reducing the inhibition returning to itself. Two successive inhibitions give positive feedback.
cards.quote: Two inhibitions in a row act as positive feedback, the switch-making arrangement from signaling circuits.

cards.front: Notch is held active in every cell of a fly proneural cluster regardless of Delta. What happens to precursor production, and why?
cards.back: No neural precursor forms: persistent Notch activity maintains E(spl) repression of the proneural genes in every cell.
cards.quote: They encode bHLH repressors that switch proneural genes off.

cards.front: Why do precursors arise at reproducible positions on the real fly notum when an idealised equal pair chooses a winner by chance?
cards.back: Proneural levels on the notum are already uneven. Lateral inhibition amplifies that pre-existing positional bias.
cards.quote: because proneural levels are already uneven before lateral inhibition acts; the loop sharpens that bias.

cards.front: What is the round-trip factor in a two-cell lateral inhibition loop?
cards.back: The product of the response factors over one complete trip from one cell through its neighbour and back.
cards.quote: The product for the whole trip, here about 5.7, is the round-trip factor.
cards.section: When does the tie break? The loop must be steep

cards.front: A system with two stable outcomes separated by an unstable even state is {{c1::bistable}}.
cards.quote: A system with two stable outcomes and an unstable even state between them is bistable.
cards.section: When does the tie break? The loop must be steep

cards.front: Why does positive feedback alone fail to guarantee that two initially similar cells adopt different fates?
cards.back: The responses must amplify the difference over a complete loop. If the returning difference is smaller, it fades and the cells remain alike.
cards.quote: Positive feedback is not, by itself, enough to split two equal cells.
cards.section: When does the tie break? The loop must be steep

cards.front: Near the even state in the two-cell model, each hand-off has gain about 2.39. What round-trip factor acts on a 1 percent Delta perturbation, and does it grow?
cards.back: Round-trip factor = G² = (2.39)² ≈ 5.7. A 1 percent perturbation returns as about 5.7 percent and grows because the factor exceeds 1.
cards.why: These are illustrative responses to a small perturbation near the even state, not measured changes or successive time steps.
cards.quote: The same two steps back to A multiply by about 2.4 again (2.39 squared is 5.73), so the 1 percent comes back as about 5.7 percent.
cards.section: When does the tie break? The loop must be steep

cards.front: In the shallow two-cell model, a 1 percent Delta difference returns as about 0.14 percent after one loop. What happens if the cells are simply left longer, and why?
cards.back: They stay alike. The loop shrinks a small difference, so waiting longer does not turn this stable even state into a split.
cards.quote: The difference fades, and the two cells stay alike however long you wait.
cards.section: When does the tie break? The loop must be steep

cards.front: In the lesson’s model, why can a lateral inhibition loop that separates a cell pair fail to produce exactly one winner in a large cluster?
cards.back: The pair and sheet have different thresholds because neighbour averaging dilutes a single cell’s influence. Even above the sheet threshold, the loop spaces winners; cluster size and shape determine their number.
cards.why: This combines the model’s geometry-dependent threshold with its distinction between spacing winners and guaranteeing one per cluster.
cards.quote: So on an extended sheet the loop spaces winners apart; it does not by itself guarantee one winner per cluster.
cards.section: When does the tie break? The loop must be steep

cards.front: Delta is lost throughout a fly embryo’s ventral neuroectoderm. What tissue imbalance results, and why?
cards.back: Too many neuroblasts and too little epidermis form. Cells cannot send the Delta signal that normally inhibits neural precursor selection in neighbours.
cards.quote: Fly embryos lacking Notch or Delta make far too many neuroblasts and too little epidermis on their underside.

cards.front: Why does a Delta-mutant fly cell beside normal cells differ from a Notch-mutant cell in its ability to receive inhibition?
cards.back: A Delta-mutant cell loses sending but retains Notch and can receive inhibition. A Notch-mutant cell cannot receive it and becomes neural on its own.
cards.quote: Losing Delta removes only what a cell sends.

cards.front: In fly mosaics, a normal cell becomes epidermis beside lower-Notch neighbours but a precursor beside higher-Notch neighbours. What model of fate choice does this challenge?
cards.back: It challenges a rule based only on the cell’s own fixed Notch level. The focal cell is normal in both cases; changing its neighbours changes its fate, supporting relative signaling through mutual inhibition.
cards.why: This combines the mosaic comparison with the rule that each cell inhibits the cell that inhibits it.
cards.quote: In these mosaics, what decided a cell's fate was how its signaling compared with that of the cells beside it.

cards.front: In a hypothetical tissue, equal numbers of border cells have lower or higher Notch receptor doses. Of 80 precursors, 60 come from the lower-dose group. What percentage is that, and what does the bias suggest?
cards.back: 60/80 × 100 = 75 percent. With equal representation, this supports a precursor advantage for cells with less Notch than their neighbours; receptor dose does not alone prove a complete mechanism.
cards.quote: A normal cell beside cells with less Notch activity than its own became epidermis, and beside cells with more Notch activity it became a neural precursor.

cards.front: Why does lateral inhibition act as a brake on neuron production in the vertebrate neural tube rather than fixing a fly-like neural–epidermal pattern?
cards.back: Inhibited vertebrate cells remain dividing neural progenitors and can differentiate later. Most inhibited fly cells instead become epidermis.
cards.quote: a cell held back here stays a dividing progenitor and can compete again later, while most of the fly's held-back cells become epidermis.
cards.section: Vertebrates: a brake and a clock

cards.front: The vertebrate relatives of fly E(spl) repressors are the {{c1::Hes}} genes.
cards.quote: The vertebrate relatives of E(spl) are the Hes genes, and Hes inhibits proneural genes.
cards.section: Vertebrates: a brake and a clock

cards.front: Hes1 is removed from mouse neural progenitors. What happens to neuronal differentiation and the progenitor pool, and why?
cards.back: Neurons appear too early and the progenitor pool is depleted as repression of proneural factors is lost. Removing Hes5 as well makes progenitor loss faster.
cards.quote: Their neural tubes expressed more Ascl1, made neurons too early, and had severe neural tube defects.
cards.section: Vertebrates: a brake and a clock

cards.front: Does finding Notch protein in two neighbouring vertebrate neural-tube progenitors identify which one will remain a progenitor?
cards.back: No. Both carry the receptor; the cell with more strongly activated Notch stays a progenitor. Receptor presence alone does not identify signaling activity.
cards.quote: Both cells have the receptor. The cell whose Notch is more strongly activated stays a progenitor;
cards.section: Vertebrates: a brake and a clock

cards.front: An optogenetic experiment in cultured mouse neural progenitors compares sustained and oscillating Ascl1 expression. What did the contrasting outcomes show?
cards.back: Sustained Ascl1 pushed differentiation into neurons; oscillating Ascl1 maintained dividing progenitors. Expression timing changes the outcome produced by the same factor.
cards.quote: Steady Ascl1 pushed cells toward becoming neurons. Oscillating Ascl1 kept them dividing as progenitors.
cards.section: Vertebrates: a brake and a clock

cards.front: How would you test whether a proneural factor’s expression timing affects differentiation independently of its average level in cultured neural progenitors?
cards.back: Compare steady and oscillating expression with matched average levels in otherwise comparable cultures, then measure division and neuronal differentiation. Different outcomes would support a timing effect beyond the average level.
cards.why: The design rests on the observed contrast between steady and oscillating proneural expression. Matching average levels tests timing as the cause.
cards.quote: The same factor gave opposite results depending on its timing.
cards.section: Vertebrates: a brake and a clock

cards.front: In a coding-region swap, which part of a gene is replaced, and which DNA controls the replacement’s expression?
cards.back: The protein-coding region is replaced; regulatory DNA at the recipient gene controls the replacement.
cards.quote: A coding-region swap puts one factor's protein-coding part at the other's gene, under the other's regulatory DNA.
cards.section: Do proneural genes carry identity? The Ascl1 and Neurog2 swap

cards.front: What do the unequal outcomes of the mouse forebrain Ascl1–Neurog2 swaps imply about neuronal identity?
cards.back: Ascl1 partly ventralized dorsal cells; Neurog2 restored ventral neurogenesis without dorsalizing it. Identity depends on both the factor and the tissue.
cards.quote: So proneural factors carry partly different identity information, and how much depends on the factor and the tissue.
cards.section: Do proneural genes carry identity? The Ascl1 and Neurog2 swap

cards.front: A hypothetical coding-region swap restores neuron production and leaves regional markers unchanged. What does it establish about the replacement factor, and what identity claim remains unsupported?
cards.back: It can support neurogenesis in that regional context. The result does not establish that the factor alone specifies regional identity; the retained markers support a role for the receiving tissue.
cards.why: This combines the separation of neuron production from subtype identity with the rule that the tissue helps determine identity.
cards.quote: A precursor's identity comes from the proneural factor together with where the cell is and what it has already been told.
cards.section: Do proneural genes carry identity? The Ascl1 and Neurog2 swap

cards.front: If Notch signaling is blocked in both fly embryonic proneural clusters and vertebrate neural progenitors, how do the expected outcomes differ, and why?
cards.back: Fly clusters produce excess neural precursors at the expense of epidermis. Vertebrate progenitors differentiate too soon, depleting the progenitor pool. In both, inhibition is lost; the difference follows from what the inhibited cells would otherwise become.
cards.why: This combines lateral inhibition with the distinct fly and vertebrate starting states and held-back fates.
cards.quote: In the vertebrate neural tube, where cells are already neural, the proneural factor pushes a progenitor toward a neuron and Notch-Hes signalling holds its neighbours back,

cards.front: DAPT blocks the final cut that releases the inner part of Notch. What happens to Notch signaling, and why?
cards.back: Notch signaling switches off because γ-secretase cannot make the membrane cut needed to release its inner signaling domain.
cards.quote: The drug DAPT, one of this lesson's structures, blocks this cut and so switches Notch off.
cards.section: The last cut is regulated proteolysis

cards.front: Why can equal messenger RNA levels for a signaling ligand fail to imply equal signaling activity?
cards.back: RNA abundance does not establish that the ligand is active. Differences in ligand activation can alter signaling even when transcript levels look similar.
cards.quote: a good part of the difference between cells may lie in Delta's activity.

cards.front: What mechanism is proposed to extend Delta signaling beyond touching neighbours on the fly notum?
cards.back: Delta-bearing filopodia could extend signaling beyond immediate neighbours, helping explain the wider spacing of sensory organ precursors.
cards.quote: The longer reach proposed is signaling beyond touching neighbours, through Delta-bearing filopodia, thin cell extensions
cards.section: Spacing, and one winner per cluster

cards.front: In the receptor-dose model, two otherwise equal cells start with equal Delta, but A has half as much Notch as B. Which becomes neural, and why?
cards.back: A becomes neural. Its lower receptor dose makes it less sensitive to inhibition, so it retains more proneural activity and sends more Delta to inhibit B.
cards.quote: if a cell's Notch activity is scaled by its share of the normal receptor, a cell with half the Notch of its partner wins

cards.front: In the illustrative receptor-dose model, nearly even pairs at half receptor dose have G ≈ 1.6; nearly even pairs at one-tenth dose have G ≈ 0.07. Calculate their round-trip factors. Is the same 1:1 dose ratio sufficient for splitting?
cards.back: At half dose, G² ≈ 1.6² = 2.56 > 1, so a small starting difference grows and the pair splits. At one-tenth dose, G² ≈ 0.07² = 0.0049 < 1, so the difference fades. A 1:1 ratio is insufficient: absolute signaling sets whether splitting occurs.
cards.why: This combines the round-trip threshold for a pair with the receptor-dose model; the numerical values are illustrative.
cards.quote: So the relative signal biases which cell wins, and the absolute signal decides whether the pair splits at all.

cards.front: In a cultured-cell experiment, blocking protein synthesis causes a regulatory gene’s oscillating messenger RNA to become persistently high. What feedback mechanism fits this result?
cards.back: The encoded protein normally represses its own gene. Blocking its synthesis removes the feedback needed to bring messenger RNA down.
cards.quote: The models agree with the experiment in which blocking protein synthesis stopped the cycle with the messenger RNA high.
cards.section: Why the Hes1 clock needs a delay

cards.front: Why are short messenger RNA and protein half-lives alone insufficient for sustained Hes1 oscillations?
cards.back: A two-step RNA–protein repression loop with steady decay settles to a steady level. Sustained cycling also needs a transcription/translation delay or extra steps.
cards.quote: but the cycle also needs the delay of transcription and translation, or extra steps in the loop.
cards.section: Why the Hes1 clock needs a delay
